body.text: Taiwan is widely seen as one of the world’s major potential flashpoints. Particularly since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, concerns have grown among observers, analysts, and policymakers in the United States, other Western countries, and the Asia-Pacific region that Beijing may take military action against Taiwan, which Beijing perceives as moving increasingly toward independence under the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) government. Xi Jinping’s increasingly assertive pursuit of cross-strait reunification has further intensified these concerns.

Why is Beijing so determined to achieve reunification with Taiwan? Despite extensive discussions in the media, academia, and policy circles outside mainland China, this question has yet to receive a sufficiently convincing answer.

A prevailing view outside China emphasizes the significant strategic and security advantages that cross-strait reunification would bring to Beijing. According to this perspective, reunification with Taiwan would enable Beijing to break through the security constraints imposed by the U.S. and its allies and extend China’s maritime defense perimeter outward. This would not only substantially strengthen Beijing’s strategic position in the Asia-Pacific region but also enhance the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) ability to project military power beyond the First Island Chain. This interpretation of Beijing’s motivation for reunification also reflects Washington’s and its regional allies’ concerns about the strategic implications of China’s control over Taiwan.

Another important motivation frequently attributed to Beijing by U.S. analysts and policymakers in recent years is the prospect of gaining control over Taiwan’s advanced semiconductor industry, particularly its leading-edge chip manufacturing capabilities, which occupy a critical position in the global semiconductor supply chain and the ongoing China-U.S. technological competition.

If these are indeed Beijing’s two primary motivations for pursuing cross-strait reunification, then, given Taiwan’s strong resistance to political incorporation under Chinese Communist Party (CCP) rule, Beijing could fully realize these two objectives only by establishing direct control over the island, most plausibly through a successful military invasion. Moreover, to achieve the objective of controlling Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, the island’s manufacturing capabilities would need to remain intact and operational following a successful invasion by the PLA.

Nevertheless, whether Beijing will ultimately resort to military force to reunify Taiwan remains uncertain, as does the question of whether such an invasion, if undertaken, would succeed. In the view of John Lee and Jan-Peter Kleinhans, “invasion likely remains at the bottom of the list for China’s leaders when sizing up solutions to the ‘Taiwan problem.’” If the use of force to reunify Taiwan is not a foregone conclusion, the only other option for Beijing to achieve both objectives would be peaceful reunification, requiring Taiwan to agree voluntarily to political incorporation into the People’s Republic of China (PRC) under CCP rule. Yet such a scenario appears highly implausible given the Taiwanese people’s strong sense of Taiwanese identity and deep-seated resentment against Beijing’s communist regime and authoritarian system.

Furthermore, historical evidence also calls these material-interest explanations into question. As late as 2001, then-Chinese leader Jiang Zemin explicitly indicated that, following reunification, Taiwan could retain its own political and economic systems and armed forces and administer its domestic affairs without the deployment of PLA troops or mainland administrative personnel on the island. Jiang’s statement suggests that direct strategic and military control over Taiwan was not an indispensable objective of Beijing’s reunification policy.

Against this background, it is difficult to argue convincingly that Beijing’s determined pursuit of reunification with Taiwan is primarily motivated by the prospect of improving its strategic and security position and gaining control over Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These are undoubtedly two advantages that reunification through a successful military invasion could potentially bring to Beijing, but they don’t seem to be the main rationale for this strategic goal. What, then, is the primary motivation behind Beijing’s determined pursuit of reunification with Taiwan in recent years, particularly under Xi Jinping?

A closer examination of Beijing’s Taiwan policy reveals that, fundamentally, the CCP views reunification with Taiwan as a nationalist issue rather than one driven primarily by material interests. In other words, cross-strait reunification is regarded first and foremost as an issue of deep national sentiment, emotion, and pride.

During his interview with CBS journalist Mike Wallace on September 2, 1986, Deng Xiaoping made this point explicit. In response to Wallace’s question, “What’s in it for Taiwan to be reunified with the mainland?” Deng explained: “First of all, it is a national question, a question of national sentiments. All members of the Chinese nation want to see China reunified. The present state of division is contrary to our national will.”

For Beijing, Taiwan embodies the Chinese people’s painful historical memories and symbolizes the nation’s “century of humiliation” stemming from the encroachment of Western and Japanese colonial powers on a weak China from the 19th century through the first half of the 20th century. Consequently, cross-strait reunification is regarded as an indispensable step toward overcoming this national trauma and an integral part of the nationalist mission of achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation by the mid-21st century. It is within this nationalist context that Beijing has consistently identified Taiwan as a “core interest” – a foreign policy principle that cannot be compromised.

In a further analysis, however, reunification with Taiwan, along with other core interests identified by the CCP leadership – including state sovereignty, territorial integrity, national security, and economic development and modernization – is subordinate to Beijing’s paramount core interest of preserving China’s existing political system, namely, the CCP’s monopoly on the nation’s political power. In other words, all other core interests ultimately serve to advance the paramount core interest of the security and preservation of the communist regime. Both Beijing’s domestic and foreign policies are fundamentally formulated to ensure regime security.

Cross-strait reunification, as a core national interest, is always used by the CCP first and foremost as an important means of enhancing the legitimacy and security of the communist regime. The other potential material benefits of reunification – such as overcoming the security constraints of the First Island Chain, extending the country’s maritime defense perimeter outward, and gaining access to Taiwan’s advanced semiconductor capabilities – are only secondary to this fundamental objective of regime security.

Particularly as China’s economic growth has slowed significantly in recent years, Beijing can no longer rely on rapid economic growth as a source of regime legitimacy to the extent that it did for nearly four decades following the launch of economic reforms in the late 1970s. Consequently, Xi now places even greater emphasis on reunification as a means of sustaining regime legitimacy and security through nationalist mobilization, particularly in the context of mounting domestic economic and social difficulties.

Along this line of thinking, it can be inferred that cross-strait reunification is pursued by Beijing to strengthen the Chinese communist regime. Thus, although Beijing appears offensive on the surface in pushing hard for a “one country, two systems” reunification, the CCP’s proposed model of reunification is fundamentally defensive in nature. Given the paramount objective of maintaining and enhancing regime legitimacy and security, Xi’s “one country, two systems” scheme is designed, on the one hand, to enhance the legitimacy of the CCP regime through reunification with Taiwan and, on the other hand, to use “two systems” as a political firewall to protect the communist regime from the potentially subversive influence of Taiwan’s democracy.

Ironically, if Taipei were to shift its policy from resisting Xi’s “one country, two systems” reunification proposal to advocating reunification under a democratic political system grounded in Sun Yat-sen’s Three Principles of the People, Beijing would find itself in a political dilemma. In his November 12, 2026 speech at a gathering commemorating the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen’s birth, Xi Jinping called for carrying forward Sun Yat-sen’s legacy and achieving complete national reunification as an integral part of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Yet would Beijing actually accept cross-strait reunification under a democratic political system based on Sun’s Three Principles of the People if such reunification were to jeopardize the CCP’s one-party rule?
This underlying political logic of the Taiwan issue appears to have received little attention from policymakers and analysts in both Washington and Taipei.
